fields.title: Permissions as a Product Feature
fields.keyTakeaway: The permissions model determines which organizations can use the product, is built on the principle of least privilege, and inaccessible features are better shown with an explanation than hidden.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: A chain asks for a cashier to see their store's orders, and a manager to see the whole chain's orders. Is this a configuration task or development work?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: The permissions model determines which organizations can use the product. Too simple — and you lose the enterprise segment. Too complex — and no one can configure it. It is designed by the product manager.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: Three maturity levels of the permissions model.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **Roles.** A fixed set: administrator, employee, guest. Simple, covers small business, hits a wall with the very first structured organization.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **Roles plus scope.** The role applies within an object: store manager, chain manager. Covers most corporate use cases.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **Flexible rules.** Permissions are described by conditions. Powerful, difficult to configure and understand, rarely needed.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: Product questions that must be resolved in any model:
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: *Who assigns permissions.* Us, the client's administrator, or both sides. *What happens upon termination.* How quickly access is revoked and who does it. *Visibility.* Can a person understand why something is unavailable to them. Hidden menu items are worse than visible ones with an explanation. *Inheritance.* Do a chain manager's permissions propagate to new stores automatically or require an action.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Separately — the **principle of least privilege**: minimum access is granted by default, and expanded explicitly. The reverse approach — granting everything and then cutting back — leaves [[excessive-privileges|excessive privileges]] permanently.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/2/2: Everything for all stores in the chain
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/3/2: Financial reports, without buyer personal data
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: The accountant role appeared upon request and turned out to be in demand by almost all chains: access to money without access to buyers.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: Permissions are assigned by the administrator on the client side. We do not participate — otherwise every HR change would go through our support.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: Revocation upon termination is the client's responsibility, and this is stated in the contract. But we added a mechanism: an employee who has not signed in for 90 days is marked as inactive, and the administrator receives a reminder.
fields.sections/3/blocks/5/text: Visibility: unavailable items are shown in gray with the label "manager permissions required". This came from support tickets — people did not understand where a section went and wrote to support.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: A flexible permissions model requires a configuration interface, and that interface is a product in its own right. It is best to start with fixed roles and expand based on real requests.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: The permissions model determines which organizations can use the product, is built on the principle of least privilege, and inaccessible features are better shown with an explanation than hidden.
